reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A paraganglioma arising from the chemoreceptor tissue of the carotid body at the carotid bifurcation
Typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, pulsatile neck mass at the angle of the jaw
The mass is classically mobile from side to side but not vertically because it is tethered to the bifurcation (Fontaine sign)
Most are benign and non-functional, but a minority secrete catecholamines or behave malignantly with nodal or distant spread
A significant proportion are familial and linked to succinate dehydrogenase gene mutations, warranting genetic assessment and screening for multiple or bilateral tumours
Imaging shows a highly vascular mass splaying the internal and external carotid arteries, producing the characteristic lyre sign on angiography
Biopsy is generally avoided because of the vascularity and bleeding risk; diagnosis relies on characteristic imaging
Surgical resection is the mainstay for suitable lesions, with radiotherapy considered for high-risk or unresectable disease, and preoperative embolisation used in selected large tumours
reference.pathophysiology: The carotid body is a small chemoreceptor organ at the carotid bifurcation that senses arterial oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH. A carotid body tumour is a paraganglioma arising from its neural crest-derived chief cells. Chronic hypoxic stimulation, such as living at high altitude, can promote hyperplasia and tumour development, and hereditary forms result from germline mutations in succinate dehydrogenase subunit genes. The tumour is intensely vascular and grows within the crotch of the bifurcation, progressively splaying and encasing the internal and external carotid arteries and potentially involving adjacent cranial nerves. Most are non-functional, but some secrete catecholamines.
additionalDifferentials: Vagal or other head and neck paraganglioma
Metastatic neck node or nerve sheath tumour
additionalInvestigations: Duplex ultrasound and CT or MR angiography demonstrating a vascular mass splaying the carotid bifurcation
Catheter angiography where detailed vascular mapping or embolisation is planned
Functional and biochemical testing for catecholamine secretion when a secretory tumour is suspected
Genetic testing (including succinate dehydrogenase genes) and screening for multifocal or bilateral disease
Cross-sectional imaging to assess local extent and identify additional paragangliomas
redFlags: Features suggesting malignant paraganglioma with regional or distant spread
Catecholamine excess with paroxysmal hypertension or arrhythmia requiring assessment before intervention
Rapid growth or new cranial nerve deficits indicating local invasion
Bilateral or familial disease prompting genetic evaluation and family screening
reference.prognosis: Most carotid body tumours are benign and slow-growing, and complete resection offers an excellent outcome, though larger lesions carry greater risk of cranial nerve injury and vascular complications. A minority are malignant, and prognosis then depends on the extent of spread and completeness of treatment.
pitfalls: Performing biopsy of a highly vascular mass and precipitating significant haemorrhage
Failing to test for catecholamine secretion before surgery in a functional tumour
Overlooking hereditary disease and the need for genetic testing and screening for additional paragangliomas
Underestimating the risk of cranial nerve injury with resection of large tumours
